## How the robustness study chose its claims {#how-the-robustness-study-chose-its-claims}

::: {.small}
- **One claim per paper**, from the first phase of SCORE: a sentence of the abstract that "ideally corresponded to one statistically significant inferential test result"
- **Four checks.** The lead team kept claims that were understandable, held only one claim, indicated the direction of the effect and had a corresponding test in the article
- **Ellipses.** An expression judged "ambiguous or rhetorical" was replaced by an ellipsis, "while preserving the original wording and the meaning of the claim"
- **No research question.** The analysts received the claim, and no research question to answer
:::

::: {.src}
Preregistration of the SCORE robustness study [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness], osf.io/4ev9t, p. 5.
:::

::: notes
The robustness study took its claims from the first phase of SCORE, in which a single claim had been traced in the abstract of each paper, ideally one that matched a single significant test. The lead team then checked each claim, keeping those that were understandable, made one claim rather than several, stated a direction and had a corresponding test in the article. A phrase judged ambiguous or rhetorical was replaced by an ellipsis, so that "dramatically increased" would become three dots and "increased", and both of the workshop's claims carry such dots. The analysts received the claim and no research question, as the preregistration states.
:::

## What an analyst received {#what-an-analyst-received}

::: {.small}
- A **published paper**, in full and not blinded, so the original estimates were in view
- Its **central claim**, in one sentence
- The **data**, or directions for fetching them
- No instructions on method: any analysis that you can defend
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
And two things that no analyst was told: **who the other analysts were**, and **what they were finding**.
:::

::: {.src}
@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness; preregistration, osf.io/4ev9t, pp. 4–5.
:::

::: notes
The robustness study gave a hundred published studies to at least five independent analysts each, and I was one of those analysts, on the paper behind the Europeanisation case study, so I can describe what arrived from the inside. We received the whole published paper, not blinded, so the original estimates were in view, which if anything pulls an analyst towards the original answer. With it came the central claim in a single sentence, and the data or directions for fetching them, which in my case meant sixteen Eurobarometer waves that I had to obtain from GESIS myself, under licence. No instruction on method arrived. [advance] Two things stayed hidden throughout, who the other analysts were and what they were finding, an isolation that gives the spread of results at the end its meaning.
:::

## The two tasks {#two-tasks-months-apart .smaller}

::: {.small}
**Task 1 – free reanalysis.** Reanalyse the claim however you see fit, then record one conclusion: evidence for the claim, evidence for the opposite, no evidence either way, or evidence for the null hypothesis.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
**Task 2 – constrained reanalysis.** Once Task 1 was in, report a single main result from the family of *z*, *t*, *F* or $\chi^2$ tests, following instructions for the claim on matters such as data selection and exclusions.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Task 1 measures whether analysts reach the same verdict. Task 2 makes their *numbers* comparable, since five answers to five different questions cannot be averaged.
:::

::: {.src}
Preregistration, osf.io/4ev9t, pp. 7–8; @AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, Methods.
:::

::: notes
The study ran in two stages. Task one left the analysis entirely to the analyst, who then recorded one of four conclusions: evidence for the claim, evidence for the opposite, no evidence either way, or evidence for the null hypothesis. [advance] Once that was submitted, task two arrived, asking for a single main result in the form of a test statistic, with instructions for the claim on matters such as which data to use and what to exclude. [advance] The two tasks measure different things. Task one asks whether independent analysts reach the same verdict, and task two whether they produce the same number, a question that can only be asked once everyone answers roughly the same question, which is what the instructions were for.
:::

## The instructions in the two case studies {#the-instructions-in-the-four-cases .smaller .deepdive run="instructions"}

::: {.fs-75}
| Case study | What the instruction of Task 2 asked |
|:----|:--------------|
| Housing | to leave the ethnic composition of the communities out of the model |
| Europeanisation | to leave out the contextual variables on EU policies and on the positions of parties, to use the positive non-materialist form of EU framing, and to measure poor economic performance by the unemployment rate |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The preregistration required the instructions to "remain circumstantial (e.g., data selection, exclusions) and never give direct instructions to the choice of statistical approach or full specification of the model". The published Methods add "choice of measurement" to the examples.
:::

::: {.src}
The record of each claim in the robustness study (osf.io/q5h2c); preregistration, osf.io/4ev9t, p. 6; @AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, Methods.
:::

::: notes
The two instructions appear here side by side in my words rather than in theirs, and on the second day you read the exact wording for your own case study. The instructions differ a good deal. The Housing instruction removes the ethnic composition of the communities and says nothing else, while the Europeanisation instruction goes further, leaving out two sets of contextual variables and choosing the measures of both the outcome and the predictor. [advance] The preregistration allowed only instructions that it called circumstantial, about data selection and exclusions, and never about the statistical approach or the full model. The published Methods add the choice of measurement to the examples, and the Europeanisation instruction, which I received myself, makes two choices of exactly that kind.
:::

## Results on a common scale {#how-a-hundred-studies-become-one-number}

::: {.small}
- Every analyst reports a test statistic in whatever form the model produces – **t**, **z**, **F**, $\chi^2$ – with its degrees of freedom or its sample size
- Each is converted to a **partial correlation** *r* and then to a standardised **Cohen's *d***, so that a regression fitted in Stata and a test computed in R can be read on one axis
- A **peer panel** judges whether each pipeline is an appropriate analysis of the claim
- Only then can you ask how far apart several defensible answers are
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Standardising makes the comparison possible, but it assumes that the analysts are estimating **the same quantity**, and that the numbers fed into each conversion count the units that carry the evidence.
:::

::: {.src}
@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, p. 136 and Methods.
:::

::: notes
Even with the question pinned down, the answers arrive in different forms, since each analyst reports the statistic that their model produces, a t, a z, an F or a chi-square, with its degrees of freedom or its sample size. The robustness study converted these statistics onto a common scale, a partial correlation and then a standardised difference, so that a regression fitted in Stata and a test computed in R could be placed on one axis. A panel of peers judged whether each analysis was appropriate for the claim, so the spread that the study reports is a spread among analyses that passed review. [advance] Putting several numbers on one axis takes two things for granted: that they estimate the same quantity, the subject of much of the second day, and that each conversion counts the units that carry the evidence, the subject of the next slides.
:::

## The conversion rules {#the-conversion-rules .smaller .deepdive run="scale"}

::: {.fs-80}
| Reported statistic | Rule of the code | The number that enters beside the statistic |
|:--|:--|:--|
| *t* | $r = t / \sqrt{t^2 + df}$ | the degrees of freedom |
| *z* | $r = \tanh\left(\lvert z \rvert / \sqrt{N - 3}\right)$, with the sign of *z* | the sample size *N* |
| $\chi^2$ | $r = \tanh\left(\sqrt{\chi^2} / \sqrt{N - 3}\right)$, never negative | the sample size *N* |
| *F* | $r = \sqrt{F / (F + df_2)}$ | the second degrees of freedom |
:::

::: {.small}
Then $d = 2r / \sqrt{1 - r^2}$, and the comparison with the original result is made on *d*, within a tolerance region of ±0.05.
:::

::: {.src}
standard_correlation_coefficient.R and cohens_d.R in github.com/marton-balazs-kovacs/multi100; @AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness [p. 136].
:::

::: notes
These are the rules of the code published by the team of the robustness study. Each statistic is first turned into a correlation, and each rule needs a second number besides the statistic, the degrees of freedom for a t or an F, and the sample size for a z or a chi-square. A chi-square carries no sign, so the correlation computed from it can never be negative, whatever the direction of the result. The correlation is then turned into a Cohen's d, and the comparison with the original study is made on d, within five hundredths either side. The article itself states that these transformations rely on assumptions that may not hold in every setting.
:::

## What the conversion assumes {#what-the-conversion-assumes .smaller}

::: {.fs-80}
| Analyst of the Europeanisation claim | Reported | What entered the conversion | *r* recorded |
|:--|:--|:--|--:|
| PRL47 | *z* = −3.59 | 394,575 respondents | −0.006 |
| C6HJR, my own analysis | *t* = −3.80 | 233 degrees of freedom of a model of country-years | −0.242 |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Almost the same statistic, and correlations about 42 times apart. Neither number is wrong for its own model. The difference comes from the conversion, which reads the units counted by the software as the units that carry the evidence.
:::

::: {.src}
The processed data of the robustness study (osf.io/q5h2c), as set out in the section on the robustness study of the page SCORE on the workshop's website.
:::

::: notes
This is one of those assumptions failing, in the case study that I know best, since one of the two rows is my own analysis. Two analysts of the Europeanisation claim reported almost the same statistic, a z of minus three point five nine and a t of minus three point eight zero, yet the correlations recorded for them differ by a factor of about forty-two, because the z was converted on the three hundred and ninety-four thousand respondents of its analysis and the t on the two hundred and thirty-three degrees of freedom of my model of country-years. [advance] Neither number is wrong for its own model. The difference comes from the conversion, which here treats every respondent as an independent test of a national unemployment rate, an assumption that is arguably too strong.
:::
